docs.title: Applied Risk Management Lab
docs.text: Analyzing financial failures, stress-testing models, and designing better decisions under uncertainty.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This lab provides a structured framework for understanding financial risk through a combination of real-world case analysis, quantitative modeling, and enterprise-level decision making.

Rather than studying risk in isolation, the lab is organized around how different types of risk emerge, interact, and ultimately shape the stability of financial institutions.

Students progress from analyzing individual failures—such as model breakdowns, liquidity crises, and operational failures—to forward-looking risk design, regulatory frameworks, and ultimately a capstone Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) assessment.

docs.title: How to Use This Lab
docs.text:
• Begin with Featured Insights to understand key risk concepts
  • Work through case studies to analyze distinct failure mechanisms
  • Complete the ERM capstone to integrate all risk dimensions

Core Progression

Case Analysis → Quant Modeling → Stress Testing → ERM Integration

docs.title: How the Lab Is Structured
docs.text:
The lab is organized into three layers:

  • Case Diagnostics — Students analyze major financial failures and identify what went wrong.
  • Quantitative Risk Modeling — Students use models to measure exposure, stress assumptions, and reveal hidden vulnerabilities.
  • Enterprise Integration — Students synthesize market, credit, liquidity, and operational risks into a unified ERM framework.

docs.title: Capstone: Enterprise Risk Management
docs.text:
Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) integrates all major forms of financial risk—market, credit, liquidity, and operational—into a unified framework for evaluating firm-wide stability.

The ERM capstone is the final integration point of the lab. After analyzing risk in isolated failures, students move to firm-wide risk architecture—where market, credit, liquidity, and operational risks interact and determine institutional resilience.

This analysis reflects real-world practices used by global banks, regulators, and Chief Risk Officers to:

  • Evaluate enterprise-wide exposure
  • Conduct integrated stress testing
  • Assess capital and liquidity adequacy
  • Support board-level decision making

docs.title: LTCM — Model Risk and Correlation Breakdown
docs.text:
Insight: Statistical models fail when assumptions break under stress.

Quant Takeaway: Volatility and correlation estimates derived from stable regimes understate joint tail risk, causing portfolio risk to increase nonlinearly under stress.

Model Implication: Risk models must be supplemented with stress scenarios and correlation breakdown assumptions, particularly before applying leverage to convergence strategies.

  • Regime shifts invalidate calibration
  • Correlations converge under stress
  • Leverage amplifies model error

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: Lehman Brothers — Liquidity and Confidence Collapse
docs.text:
Insight: Institutions fail when funding disappears—not when capital first appears insufficient.

Quant Takeaway: Balance sheet solvency metrics remained relatively stable, while effective liquidity risk increased discontinuously due to funding withdrawal and valuation uncertainty.

Model Implication: Risk management frameworks must treat liquidity as a binding constraint and incorporate funding stress scenarios alongside capital adequacy measures.

  • Capital vs balance-sheet vulnerability
  • Liquidity vs solvency breakdown
  • Confidence erosion drives collapse

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: London Whale — VaR Failure and Tail Risk
docs.text:
Insight: Measuring probability of loss is not the same as understanding magnitude.

Quant Takeaway: VaR remains insensitive to tail severity, while Expected Shortfall reveals substantially larger losses under stress scenarios, indicating hidden downside exposure.

Model Implication: Institutions should rely on tail-sensitive metrics such as Expected Shortfall and explicitly manage concentration risk rather than relying solely on VaR thresholds.

  • VaR vs Expected Shortfall (ES)
  • Tail risk revealed under stress
  • Model limitations exposed

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: Global Financial Crisis — Systemic Risk Interaction
docs.text:
Insight: Systemic crises occur when multiple risk models fail simultaneously.

Quant Takeaway: CDS-implied risk (~4% for BBB), structural credit signals (Z ≈ distress), and portfolio models (WCDR ≈ 3%, CVA ≈ $52.8k) diverge significantly under stress, signaling model breakdown.

Model Implication: Risk management must integrate credit, market, liquidity, and counterparty models rather than relying on any single framework.

  • CDS vs historical PD divergence
  • Altman Z reveals hidden fragility
  • VaR underestimates systemic loss
  • CVA exposes counterparty risk
  • Wrong-way risk amplifies losses

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: Knight Capital — Operational and Model Risk Failure
docs.text:
Insight: Operational failures in automated trading systems can generate catastrophic losses within minutes.

Quant Takeaway: Knight accumulated ~$7B in unintended positions and incurred ~$440M in losses within 45 minutes due to faulty code deployment.

Model Implication: Robust governance, testing, and real-time controls are essential when models operate at high speed and scale.

  • Faulty deployment activated dormant test code
  • Lack of change control and validation under SR 11‑7
  • Positive feedback loops amplified price distortions
  • Losses driven by forced liquidation under adverse price impact
  • Operational risk manifests as a financial risk in real time

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: Sunrise National Bank — Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
docs.text:
Insight: Stress testing reveals vulnerabilities that are not observable under baseline or historical conditions.

Quant Takeaway: Under stress scenarios, SNB’s CET1 ratio declines sharply (≈4.8%, ≈3.1%, ≈4.3%), with the supervisory scenario breaching regulatory minimums and losses driven primarily by credit exposure.

Model Implication: Risk management must rely on forward-looking scenario analysis and integrate credit, market, and liquidity interactions rather than relying on static capital ratios.

  • Capital adequacy diverges significantly under stress conditions
  • Credit losses dominate total losses across scenarios
  • Market and liquidity shocks amplify capital deterioration
  • Reverse stress testing identifies non-linear failure thresholds
  • Scenario design captures interaction effects across risk categories

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: Atlas Bank International — Basel Regulation and Risk Transformation
docs.text:
Insight: Regulatory frameworks shape how risk is measured and can create incentives that amplify systemic vulnerabilities.

Quant Takeaway: ABI’s pre-crisis VaR (~$35–42M) failed to capture realized losses that escalated to ~$4.5B during the financial crisis, while Basel II.5 increased trading-book capital requirements to over $3B under stressed conditions.

Model Implication: Risk management must supplement internal models with stressed risk measures, capital buffers, and liquidity constraints to prevent underestimation of tail risk and excessive leverage.

  • Basel I enabled regulatory arbitrage through coarse risk weights
  • Basel II internal models underestimated risk during low-volatility periods
  • VaR failed to capture extreme tail losses during the crisis
  • Basel II.5 introduced sVaR, IRC, and CRM to correct trading-book weaknesses
  • Basel III strengthened CET1, leverage constraints, and liquidity standards

Further Analysis: View Executive Summary

docs.title: About the Author

Zachary Smith is an Associate Professor of Finance and Economics with a background in quantitative finance, including six years as a trading-focused analyst at Merrill Lynch across structured products, equities, fixed income, and hedge fund strategies. The Applied Risk Management Lab was created to bridge academic instruction and real-world financial decision-making through case analysis, quantitative modeling, and enterprise risk frameworks.

The design emphasizes a structured progression:

  • Diagnosing real-world financial failures
  • Understanding risk measurement and modeling limitations
  • Applying forward-looking and regulatory frameworks
  • Integrating risk at the enterprise level through ERM

The goal is to prepare students to think and act like risk professionals—capable of interpreting complex data, identifying vulnerabilities, and making informed decisions under uncertainty.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Atlas Bank International (ABI) case examines how global banking regulation evolved from Basel I to Basel III and how those changes transformed bank risk profiles, capital structures, and strategic decisions.

ABI is a large, globally active bank with significant exposure to structured credit, trading activities, and short-term funding markets.

Before the financial crisis, ABI relied heavily on:

  • Proprietary trading
  • Structured credit positions (CDOs)
  • Short-term repo funding
  • Off-balance sheet exposures

This case follows ABI through:

  • Regulatory arbitrage under Basel I
  • Model-driven risk under Basel II
  • Crisis-driven failures
  • Regulatory reforms (Basel II.5 and Basel III)
  • Strategic transformation

docs.title: Analytical Focus
docs.text:
• Evolution of Basel I → II → II.5 → III
  • Model risk and regulatory arbitrage
  • Trading-book failures and VaR limitations
  • Capital adequacy and liquidity requirements
  • Strategic responses by bank leadership

docs.title: Analytical Lens
docs.text:
Insight: Changes in regulation fundamentally reshape how risk is measured, capitalized, and managed within financial institutions.

Quant Takeaway: ABI’s VaR (~$35–42M pre-crisis) dramatically understated realized losses (~$200M to ~$4.5B), revealing severe model failure and insufficient capital under Basel II.

Model Implication: Effective risk management requires robust capital, stressed risk measures, and liquidity constraints, rather than reliance on internal models calibrated to stable periods.

Stage 1: Introducing ABI and Basel I¶
Introducing Atlas Bank International (ABI)¶
docs.text:
ABI is a globally active, aggressively trading universal bank with major exposures in structured credit, equities, commodities, and rates. Its business model before the financial crisis relied heavily on:

  • large proprietary trading desks,
  • warehousing mezzanine and equity tranches of CDOs,
  • short-term repo funding,
  • heavy use of off–balance sheet vehicles.

Basel I: Foundations and FlawsBasel I (1988) introduced the first global framework for bank capital, requiring total capital of at least 8% of Risk-Weighted Assets (RWA). However:

  • Risk weights were simple and coarse.
  • All corporate loans received 100% risk weight regardless of credit quality.
  • Off–balance sheet exposures were underestimated. ABI exploited these weaknesses through regulatory arbitrage, shifting into higher-yielding but riskier assets without requiring more capital.

docs.title: Stage 2: Basel II - Internal Models and Hidden Vulnerabilities¶
docs.text:
Basel II introduced the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approach allowing banks like ABI to estimate PD, LGD, EAD. Calm period data from 2003-2006 led to underestimated risk.

  • Procyclicality Low volatility reduced VaR despite growing exposures.
  • Supervisory IssuesBacktesting rarely failed; stress testing was inconsistent.
  • ABI Pre-crisisTrading book expanded; VaR ~42M.

Under Basel II, Atlas Bank International (ABI) utilized the Internal Ratings-Based (IRB) approach, which allowed them to estimate key risk parameters like Probability of Default (PD), Loss Given Default (LGD), and Exposure At Default (EAD. However, ABI's VaR (Value at Risk) calculations were flawed. The estimations were based on calm period data from 2003-2006, leading to an underestimation of actual risk. This also contributed to procyclicality, where low volatility reduced VaR despite increasing exposures. Furthermore, supervisory issues were present, with backtesting rarely failing and stress testing being inconsistent. Prior to the crisis, ABI's trading book expanded significantly, and its VaR was approximately $42 million.

docs.title: Stage 3: Crisis Hits ABI¶
docs.text:
• Full-Scale Market ShockWhen markets turned in 2007-08, volatility surged, credit spreads widened, and ABI's trading positions suffered severe losses far beyond VaR predictions.
  • Funding liquidity evaporated; repo haircuts jumped.
  • Margin calls forced asset fire-sales, amplifying losses.
  • Structured credit, rates, equities, and commodities desks all posted deep losses.

The 'ABI: VaR vs. Realized Losses' plot illustrates the stark difference between Atlas Bank International's (ABI) Value at Risk (VaR) estimates and its actual realized losses during the financial crisis. As the plot shows, ABI's VaR values, represented by the blue line, were relatively low and slowly increasing from 2006 to 2008 (38M, 42M, 50M respectively). In contrast, the realized losses, shown by the orange line, were significantly higher and rapidly escalated during the crisis, going from 200M in 2006 to 4500M in 2008. This indicates that ABI's VaR models severely underestimated the potential for losses, particularly the tail risk, during periods of market stress, leading to massive unexpected financial damage.

docs.title: Stage 4: Basel II.5¶
docs.text:
• Emergency Market Risk Reinforcement: Basel II.5 was created to address clear modeling failures exposed during the crisis. ABI's trading losses revealed VaR severely underestimated tail risk.
  • Stressed VaR (sVaR): Uses a fixed 250-day crisis window, forcing capital to reflect stressed conditions.
  • Incremental Risk Charge (IRC): Captures credit migration and default risk for traded credit products.
  • Comprehensive Risk Measure (CRM): Applied to correlation trading positions which suffered significant losses during the crisis.
  • ABI ImpactTrading-book capital requirements exceeded $3B under Basel II.5.

The 'ABI VaR vs Stressed VaR' plot illustrates the difference between ABI's traditional VaR and the newly introduced Stressed VaR (sVaR) under Basel II.5. Basel II.5 was created to address the clear modeling failures exposed during the crisis, where ABI's trading losses revealed that VaR severely underestimated tail risk. Stressed VaR uses a fixed 250-day crisis window, which forces capital requirements to reflect stressed conditions, typically resulting in higher values compared to regular VaR. For example, the plot shows that while VaR was relatively low (38M, 42M, 50M for 2006, 2007, 2008 respectively), Stressed VaR was significantly higher (120M, 140M, 160M for the same years), indicating a more conservative and realistic assessment of risk during turbulent periods.

docs.title: Stage 5: Basel III¶
docs.text:
• Full System Rebuild: Basel III strengthened capital quality (CET1), introduced buffers, leverage ratio, LCR, NSFR.
  • ET1 and Buffers: Higher standards for equity capital.
  • Leverage Ratio: A non-risk-based backstop.
  • Liquidity Standards: LCR ensures 30-day stress survival; NSFR ensures stable funding.
  • ABI Impact: ABI had to raise CET1, extend funding maturity, increase HQLA.

Visualizations:

First, there is a bar chart comparing Basel II and Basel III capital requirements. This plot shows the differences in minimum capital ratios for CET1 (Common Equity Tier 1), Tier 1, and Total Capital under the two regulatory frameworks. As per Basel III, the requirements are higher across the board (CET1: 7%, Tier1: 8.5%, Total: 10.5%) compared to Basel II (CET1: 4.5%, Tier1: 6%, Total: 8%), reflecting the enhanced capital quality and quantity standards introduced by Basel III.

The second plot displays ABI LCR Components. This bar chart shows the values for 'HQLA' (High-Quality Liquid Assets) at 410 and 'Outflows' at 380. This plot visually represents the key components of the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) for ABI, indicating its ability to cover short-term liquidity needs. A higher HQLA relative to outflows suggests a stronger liquidity position, which is a critical aspect of Basel III's focus on liquidity standards.

docs.title: Stage 6: Strategic Implications Under Basel III¶
docs.text:
ABI must restructure: shrink trading book, increase HQLA, extend funding maturity, pivot to fee income.

  • Trading Book ReductionHigh capital charges force reduction.
  • Funding Structure OptimizationShift to long-term debt.
  • Liquidity EnhancementLCR and NSFR reshape liquidity profile.

The visualization in Stage 6 is titled 'ABI Balance Sheet Transformation'. This bar chart illustrates the strategic changes ABI undertook in its balance sheet composition due to the implementation of Basel III. It compares the asset allocation 'Before' and 'After' these changes:

  • Trading Assets: Reduced from 600 ('Before') to 300 ('After'). This significant reduction reflects the impact of Basel III's higher capital charges on trading book activities, forcing ABI to shrink its exposure in this area.
  • Loans: Slightly increased from 400 ('Before') to 450 ('After'). This indicates a possible shift towards traditional lending, which might have more stable risk profiles or lower capital requirements compared to trading.
  • HQLA (High-Quality Liquid Assets): Substantially increased from 100 ('Before') to 300 ('After'). This critical change shows ABI's response to Basel III's new liquidity standards, such as the LCR and NSFR, by increasing its holdings of highly liquid assets to better withstand liquidity shocks.

docs.text:
Decision Branches:

  • Raise CET1 via equity issuance or deleveraging.
  • Increase HQLA or reduce risky trading positions.
  • Exit or scale down correlation trading.Each decision impacts capital, leverage, and liquidity metrics.

The 'Impact of CRO Decisions on ABI Stability' plot is a bar chart that illustrates the relative impact of various strategic decisions a Chief Risk Officer (CRO) at ABI might consider under Basel III. Each bar represents a different option, and its height indicates a numerical 'impact' value. While the specific units or scale of 'impact' are not defined in the plot, it suggests a qualitative or quantitative measure of how much each decision contributes to ABI's overall stability.

Here's what each bar signifies:

  • Raise Equity (Impact: 3): This decision likely refers to increasing Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) through new equity issuance. It contributes to stability by strengthening the bank's capital base.
  • Deleverage (Impact: 2): This involves reducing the bank's overall debt or asset size relative to its equity. It improves stability by lowering financial risk and meeting leverage ratio requirements.
  • Increase HQLA (Impact: 4): This means increasing holdings of High-Quality Liquid Assets. It directly enhances liquidity, a key focus of Basel III, allowing the bank to withstand short-term funding stresses.
  • Reduce Trading (Impact: 5): This involves shrinking the trading book. It has the highest 'impact' score, suggesting that reducing exposure to risky trading positions, which were a major source of losses during the crisis, is highly effective in improving ABI's stability under the stricter capital charges of Basel III.

Executive Summary
docs.text:
The Atlas Bank International case illustrates how regulatory frameworks and internal risk models can jointly fail to capture the true level of risk exposure in financial institutions.

Despite appearing well-capitalized under Basel II, ABI incurred massive losses during the financial crisis due to weaknesses in Value-at-Risk (VaR) models, inadequate treatment of tail risk, and reliance on short-term funding.

docs.title: Core Problem
docs.text:
At the center of the failure was a combination of:

  • Overreliance on internal risk models calibrated to low-volatility periods
  • Regulatory arbitrage under simplified capital frameworks
  • Underestimation of trading-book and structured credit risk
  • Inadequate integration of liquidity risk into capital metrics

docs.title: Analytical Approach
docs.text:
Using a stylized global bank, the analysis evaluates:

  • Evolution of capital regulation across Basel I, II, II.5, and III
  • Performance of VaR models relative to realized losses
  • Changes in trading-book capital requirements under stress measures
  • Impact of liquidity and funding constraints on balance sheet structure

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• VaR significantly underestimated losses during stress conditions
  • Realized trading losses exceeded modeled risk by a wide margin
  • Basel II.5 introduced stressed risk measures that materially increased capital requirements
  • Basel III strengthened capital quality, leverage constraints, and liquidity regulation

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text: Risk frameworks do not just measure risk—they shape behavior, and flawed frameworks can amplify systemic vulnerabilities.

docs.title: Implications for Risk Management
docs.text:
• Risk models must incorporate stress scenarios and tail risk conditions
  • Capital requirements should reflect both model-based and non-model risks
  • Liquidity constraints must be integrated into risk frameworks
  • Regulatory design must minimize incentives for risk transfer and arbitrage

:This analysis is the capstone project for FIN 520: Risk Analysis, where students synthesize all concepts learned throughout the course to evaluate the risk profile of an aggressive, derivatives‑heavy global bank. In professional practice, global banks operate complex portfolios that expose them to multiple categories of financial risk—market, credit, liquidity, operational, model, and strategic risks. Effective Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) requires integrating these risks into a unified picture that supports decision‑making by senior leadership and regulators.

Throughout FIN 520, students have learned tools for quantifying and interpreting risk using Python, including:

  • Market risk measurement through historical Value‑at‑Risk (VaR), Expected Shortfall (ES), and Monte Carlo simulation.
  • Credit risk modeling through Probability of Default (PD), Loss Given Default (LGD), Exposure at Default (EAD), Expected Loss (EL), and stress‑scenario adjustments.
  • Operational risk estimation using frequency/severity models such as Poisson–Lognormal.
  • Liquidity risk evaluation with maturity ladders, High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA), and survival horizon concepts under stressed outflows.
  • ERM dashboards and heatmaps that combine severity and likelihood across risk categories.
  • Stress testing that integrates market, credit, liquidity, and operational dynamics.

This capstone project simulates the kind of analysis conducted inside leading institutions such as large U.S. bank holding companies, European universal banks, and global investment banks, where risk managers routinely evaluate firm‑wide vulnerability under adverse conditions. The project mirrors the expectations of:

  • Basel III/IV regulatory frameworks around capital and liquidity
  • CCAR/DFAST‑style stress testing
  • Internal risk appetite and governance frameworks used by bank boards
  • Risk dashboards used by Chief Risk Officers (CROs)

To create a realistic environment without relying on proprietary bank data, the analysis uses:

  • Synthetic but economically plausible market data, representing four large bank-equity time series
  • Synthetic aggressive credit exposures, designed to mimic concentrated loan books, leveraged lending, CRE exposure, and emerging‑market sovereign risk
  • Operational risk simulations that capture heavy‑tailed behavior often observed in real incident data
  • Liquidity stress structures that reflect short‑term wholesale funding risk
  • Monte Carlo simulations representing portfolio return distributions with both normal and heavy‑tailed dynamics

Together, these components form a holistic ERM assessment that integrates:

  • Market risk shocks
  • Credit portfolio deterioration
  • Liquidity pressures
  • Operational shocks
  • Inter-risk amplification effects
  • ERM severity-likelihood visualization
  • Strategic recommendations presented at a board level

The culminating deliverable—whether a full notebook, a written narrative, or a board-style presentation—is designed to mimic the real responsibilities of risk teams who must:

  • Quantify risks
  • Interpret results
  • Communicate implications to senior leadership
  • Recommend actionable responses consistent with the bank’s risk appetite and with responsible stewardship, a core value in the Saint Leo curriculum

This analysis therefore represents the most complete integration of quantitative methods, conceptual understanding, and professional communication in the course.

1. Imports & Synthetic Market Data (Financial Analytics Style)¶
docs.text: Stock price changes give us volatility, correlation, and return distributions — the core ingredients of market risk measurement. They also act as early-warning signals of financial stress and integrate directly with liquidity pressure, credit deterioration, and systemic contagion. Without them, a global bank’s ERM analysis would be blind to the primary market drivers of losses and stress‑test outcomes.

docs.title: Historical VaR and ES as Dollar Amounts (assuming $1 Billion Portfolio)¶
docs.text: We model a $1 billion portfolio because it is large enough to produce meaningful market, credit, liquidity, and operational losses — the same order of magnitude monitored inside global banks. This scale gives realistic dollar values to VaR, ES, expected loss, and stress‑scenario outcomes, allowing students to perform a fully integrated, board‑level ERM assessment rather than a toy example.

docs.title: Portfolio Dollar Changes — Historical Distribution with VaR and ES in Dollars¶
3. Market Risk — Monte Carlo VaR (Normal + t-distribution)¶
4. Credit Risk — PD, LGD, EAD, Expected Loss¶
docs.text: In the credit risk section, we quantify expected losses across loan segments using PD (likelihood of default), LGD (loss severity), and EAD (exposure at default). Expected Loss = PD × LGD × EAD gives us the baseline credit losses the bank expects under normal conditions. These values scale credit risk in dollars, feed into stress testing under adverse scenarios, and become part of the integrated ERM dashboard.

docs.title: 5. Operational Risk — Poisson-Lognormal Simulation¶
docs.text: The operational risk section simulates the frequency and severity of internal failures, fraud, system breakdowns, and external shocks using a Poisson–Lognormal model. This generates a realistic distribution of annual OpRisk losses, characterized by many small losses and occasional catastrophic tail events. The mean and 99% tail metrics are then integrated into the ERM Dashboard, giving a full view of the bank’s vulnerability beyond market and credit factors.

docs.title: 6. Liquidity Maturity Ladder & Survival Horizon¶
docs.text:
The liquidity maturity ladder shows the bank’s net cash inflows and outflows across different time buckets, highlighting when liquidity pressure is greatest. The survival horizon measures how long the bank can meet these outflows using its High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA). This helps identify near‑term liquidity vulnerabilities, a key component of ERM because liquidity crises often unfold faster and more severely than market or credit stress.

Note: The 1B portfolio represents the bank’s market‑risk trading book, not the entire firm. Liquidity risk is measured across all business lines, including deposits, wholesale funding, repo markets, derivatives collateral, and payment obligations. Global banks routinely experience tens of billions of weekly cash flows, regardless of the size of their trading book. Therefore, liquidity outflows of 30B in the 0–7 day bucket reflect the full balance-sheet liquidity profile, not the size of the trading portfolio.

This distinction is essential: A bank can have a small trading book but still face enormous short‑term liquidity needs — and this mismatch is often what triggers liquidity crises.

docs.title: 7. ERM Dashboard¶
docs.text: The ERM Dashboard consolidates market, credit, liquidity, and operational risk into a single severity‑versus‑likelihood matrix. This allows the bank to identify which risks are most threatening, prioritize management action, and ensure alignment with the risk appetite. The heatmap provides a board‑level view of total enterprise risk, combining quantitative analytics with strategic judgment.

docs.title: Summary##¶
docs.text:
This Module 8 capstone brings together all major forms of financial risk—market, credit, liquidity, and operational—into a single, integrated Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) framework similar to those used by global banks and regulatory bodies. The purpose of the analysis is to show students how different risk types interact, how losses across business lines accumulate, and how risk managers produce a unified, decision‑relevant picture for senior leadership.

To anchor the analysis in realistic scale, we model a $1 billion trading portfolio, which feeds market‑risk measures such as Value‑at‑Risk (VaR), Expected Shortfall (ES), correlation structures, heavy‑tailed Monte Carlo simulations, and stress‑scenario impacts. This portfolio represents the bank’s risk‑sensitive trading book—not the entire institution—allowing us to study market losses in a controlled, interpretable way.

Credit risk is modeled through PD, LGD, and EAD across four loan portfolio segments, producing Expected Loss (EL), a baseline measure of credit deterioration. These results illustrate how concentrations in CRE, consumer lending, or emerging markets can materially affect the bank’s overall risk profile.

Operational risk is captured using a Poisson–Lognormal frequency/severity model, which mimics real‑world operational risk behavior: many small losses punctuated by occasional catastrophic events. The 99th‑percentile tail loss gives a realistic sense of exposure to misconduct, fraud, system failures, cyber events, or fines.

Liquidity risk is evaluated through a liquidity maturity ladder and survival horizon, which reveal how quickly the bank can meet cash outflows using its High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA). Large short‑term liquidity needs—common in wholesale‑funded global banks—illustrate one of the fastest pathways to bank failure. This section shows how a bank can be solvent but still collapse due to short‑term liquidity pressures.

The ERM Dashboard consolidates these risks into a unified severity × likelihood matrix, revealing which exposures pose the greatest threat. This dashboard mirrors the tools used by Chief Risk Officers (CROs) and Board Risk Committees to set risk appetite, adjust capital buffers, and prioritize management attention. By placing every risk—market, credit, liquidity, and operational—side by side, the dashboard provides a holistic view that no individual risk silo can convey.

Together, these components form a complete ERM workflow. Students see how market volatility affects liquidity, how credit deterioration interacts with funding stress, and how operational risk tail events can materially worsen losses during downturns. The final board‑ready summary and recommendations require students to synthesize quantitative results into strategic insights—mirroring real‑world responsibilities of risk managers in global financial institutions.

# --- Helper Functions ---

def hazard_rate(spread_bps: float, recovery: float) -> float:
    # Risk-neutral average annual default probability (hazard rate) ~ s / (1 - R).
    s = spread_bps / 10000.0
    return s / (1 - recovery)


def altman_z(financials: dict) -> float:
    # Altman Z-Score for manufacturing firms (classic 5-factor version).
    X1 = financials['WC'] / financials['TA']
    X2 = financials['RE'] / financials['TA']
    X3 = financials['EBIT'] / financials['TA']
    X4 = financials['MVE'] / financials['Liab']
    X5 = financials['Sales'] / financials['TA']
    Z = 1.2*X1 + 1.4*X2 + 3.3*X3 + 0.6*X4 + 1.0*X5
    return Z


def vasicek_wcdr(PD: float, rho: float, X: float) -> float:
    # Worst-Case Default Rate at confidence level X under Vasicek single-factor model.
    from scipy.stats import norm
    return norm.cdf((norm.ppf(PD) + (rho**0.5)*norm.ppf(X)) / (1 - rho)**0.5)

    total = 0.0

X1 = financials['WC'] / financials['TA'] X2 = financials['RE'] / financials['TA'] X3 = financials['EBIT'] / financials['TA'] X4 = financials['MVE'] / financials['Liab'] X5 = financials['Sales'] / financials['TA'] Z = 1.2*X1 + 1.4*X2 + 3.3*X3 + 0.6*X4 + 1.0*X5 return Z def vasicek_wcdr(PD: float, rho: float, X: float) -> float: # Worst-Case Default Rate at confidence level X under Vasicek single-factor model. from scipy.stats import norm return norm.cdf((norm.ppf(PD) + (rho**0.5)*norm.ppf(X)) / (1 - rho)**0.5) def cva(exposures: list, q: list, R: float, df: float) -> pd.DataFrame: # Compute per-year and total CVA with flat annual discounting df^i. rows = [] total = 0.0 for i, (V, qi) in enumerate(zip(exposures, q), start=1): DF_i = df**i V_pv = V * DF_i LGD = (1 - R) CVA_i = LGD * qi * V_pv total += CVA_i rows.append({'Year': i, 'Exposure': V, 'DF_i': DF_i, 'Exposure_PV': V_pv, 'q_i': qi, 'LGD': LGD, 'CVA_i': CVA_i}) import numpy as np import pandas as pd df_out = pd.DataFrame(rows) df_out.loc[len(df_out)] = {'Year': 'Total', 'Exposure': np.nan, 'DF_i': np.nan, 'Exposure_PV': df_out['Exposure_PV'].sum(), 'q_i': np.nan, 'LGD': (1-R), 'CVA_i': total} return df_out print('Helper functions loaded')

The Python code in Task 5 simulates a trading glitch scenario, similar to the Knight Capital incident, by generating initial stock prices, calculating a sudden price 'jump' (increase), and then deriving new, affected prices. It utilizes numpy for efficient numerical operations and matplotlib for data visualization.

Here's a breakdown of each part:

  1. Generating Initial Stock Prices (prices):

    prices = np.random.uniform(20, 200, 50)

    This line uses numpy.random.uniform(low, high, size) to create an array named prices. It generates 50 (specified by size=50) random floating-point numbers, each uniformly distributed between a low value of 20 and a high value of 200. This array represents the initial, pre-glitch stock prices for 50 different hypothetical stocks.

  2. Calculating the Price 'Jump' (jump):

    jump = prices * np.random.uniform(0.05, 0.25, 50)

    To simulate a sudden price increase (a 'jump'), this line calculates jump by taking the prices array and multiplying each initial price by a random percentage. np.random.uniform(0.05, 0.25, 50) generates another array of 50 random values, this time between 0.05 (5%) and 0.25 (25%). When multiplied by prices, this effectively creates an array where each element represents a random percentage increase (between 5% and 25%) of its corresponding initial stock price. This simulates the unintended buying pressure and subsequent price distortion seen in market glitches.

  3. Deriving New Prices (newp):

    newp = prices + jump

    This line calculates the newp array, which represents the stock prices after the glitch. It does this by simply adding the calculated jump (the price increase) to the original prices array. Each element in newp is the sum of an initial price and its corresponding jump, showing the inflated price due to the simulated glitch.

  4. Role of numpy: numpy (Numerical Python) is fundamental here for its ability to perform fast and efficient array operations. Instead of using Python loops, which would be much slower for large datasets, numpy allows vectorized operations (like element-wise multiplication and addition on entire arrays). This makes the code concise, readable, and highly performant for numerical computations, which is crucial in financial modeling and simulations involving large amounts of data.

  5. Plotting the Changes with matplotlib:

    plt.plot(prices); plt.plot(newp); plt.show()

    matplotlib.pyplot (aliased as plt) is used for visualizing the data. The first plt.plot(prices) command plots the initial stock prices, and the second plt.plot(newp) command plots the new, post-glitch prices on the same graph. By plotting both, the user can visually compare the original prices with the prices after the simulated glitch, clearly showing the 'jump'. Finally, plt.show() displays the generated plot.

docs.text: On August 1, 2012, Knight Capital — then one of the largest U.S. equity market makers — deployed new code intended to interact with the NYSE's Retail Liquidity Program. However, a dormant testing module (called Power Peg) was accidentally reactivated. When markets opened, this module sent millions of unintended buy and sell orders across 150+ stocks, causing Knight to accumulate nearly 7 billion in unintended positions within 45 minutes. According to reports, this resulted in losses of approximately 440 million as Knight unwound the positions.

docs.title: Why This is a Model Risk Event¶
docs.text: Even though the failure was software-driven, it represents a textbook case of model risk: deploying untested logic, lack of governance, inadequate change management, and absence of independent verification.

docs.title: Explanation of Loss Reconstruction¶
docs.text:
This section calculates the estimated financial loss incurred by Knight Capital due to the trading glitch. The calculation is based on the following variables:

  • purchase: Represents the estimated total value of the unintended positions accumulated by Knight Capital. In this case, it's set to $7 billion (7,000,000,000).
  • impact_up: Represents the upward price impact (percentage increase) on the stocks as Knight Capital bought them, inadvertently driving prices higher. This is set to 2.5% (0.025).
  • impact_down: Represents the downward price impact (percentage decrease) on the stocks as Knight Capital unwound its positions, selling them and driving prices lower. This is set to 3.5% (0.035).
  • loss: This variable calculates the total financial loss. It is determined by multiplying the purchase amount by the sum of impact_up and impact_down. The sum of impact_up and impact_down represents the total percentage price movement (both positive and negative) that contributed to the loss during the buying and selling process.

The formula used is loss = purchase * (impact_up + impact_down). This means that the total loss is a direct result of the large volume of trades (purchase) and the combined adverse price movements (impact_up + impact_down) experienced during the incident.

docs.title: Explanation of the 'Distribution of Potential Losses' Plot¶
docs.text:
This histogram visualizes the frequency of different potential loss amounts based on a log-normal distribution, often used to model financial risks.

  • X-axis (Loss ($)): Represents the magnitude of potential losses in U.S. dollars. It shows a wide range, from smaller, more frequent losses to larger, less frequent ones.
  • Y-axis (Frequency (log scale)): Shows how often each loss amount occurs. The use of a logarithmic scale allows for better visualization of events that occur with vastly different frequencies. This is particularly useful for 'tail risk' events, which are rare but have a significant impact.

Key Takeaway: The plot illustrates a typical log-normal distribution, characterized by a long right tail. This indicates that while most potential losses might be relatively small, there is a distinct, albeit low, probability of experiencing extremely large losses (known as 'tail risk'). This is critical for understanding and managing financial risk, as these extreme events can have disproportionate impacts, as seen in the Knight Capital incident.

docs.title: Explanation of the 'Glitch Simulation' Plot¶
docs.text:
This plot visually represents a simulated market glitch, akin to what occurred during the Knight Capital incident, by showing the immediate impact on stock prices. It displays two distinct lines:

  • Blue Line ('prices'): Represents the original, underlying prices of 50 different stocks before the glitch occurred. These are the baseline prices.
  • Orange Line ('newp'): Represents the new, increased prices of the same 50 stocks after the simulated glitch. This line shows the prices after an 'unintended jump' has been applied.

Visualizing the Glitch's Impact: The plot clearly demonstrates the immediate and widespread effect of the simulated glitch. For every stock, the orange line ('newp') is consistently above the blue line ('prices'), illustrating a rapid and unintended upward shift in prices across the board. This 'jump' in prices is a direct visual representation of how erroneous trading algorithms, like the one at Knight Capital, can instantaneously inflate asset values due to massive, unwarranted buy orders.

Relevance to Knight Capital: This visualization directly parallels the market disruption experienced by Knight Capital. The original 'prices' can be thought of as the stable market before August 1, 2012. The 'newp' represents the prices as Knight Capital's Power Peg module sent millions of unintended orders, driving prices significantly higher. The plot effectively illustrates the rapid, unintended price movements and the immediate market distortion that such technical malfunctions can cause, leading to massive financial losses as positions are accumulated at artificially inflated prices.

Within minutes of deployment, faulty code generated millions of erroneous trades, leading to approximately $7 billion in unintended positions and ~$440 million in losses.

This notebook simulates a simplified credit derivatives portfolio inspired by the JPMorgan London Whale incident.

We will:

  • Generate synthetic daily returns for a CDS portfolio.

docs.title: Historical Context: The JPMorgan London Whale Incident¶
docs.text:
The 'London Whale' incident refers to a significant trading loss incurred by JPMorgan Chase in 2012. A trader in the bank's London office, Bruno Iksil (nicknamed the 'London Whale' due to the size of his trades), made massive bets on credit default swaps (CDS). These positions were so large they moved the market, and when the market turned against them, the losses mounted rapidly, eventually totaling over $6 billion.

Key issues and lessons learned from this event include:

  • Flawed Risk Models: JPMorgan Chase's Value-at-Risk (VaR) models, like those we're simulating here, severely underestimated the potential losses. The models did not adequately capture the tail risk or the illiquidity of the markets for such large positions.
  • Concentration Risk: The sheer size of Iksil's positions meant that a single trader could have a disproportionate impact on the bank's overall risk profile.
  • Lack of Oversight: There was a failure in the bank's internal controls and oversight mechanisms to detect and curb the excessive risk-taking in a timely manner.
  • Regulatory Scrutiny: The incident led to increased scrutiny from regulators globally, contributing to stricter regulations under Basel III and the Dodd-Frank Act, particularly regarding capital requirements and stress testing for banks.

In essence, the London Whale incident highlighted how even sophisticated financial institutions could suffer massive losses due to inadequacies in their risk management frameworks, especially their reliance on metrics like VaR which can fail to predict extreme tail events. It underscored the critical importance of robust risk management and the use of more comprehensive metrics like Expected Shortfall (CVaR) to capture extreme potential losses.

docs.title: JPMorgan London Whale (2012) — Tail Risk and Model Failure
Executive Summary
docs.text:
The JPMorgan London Whale incident illustrates how sophisticated risk models can obscure, rather than reveal, true risk exposure when applied without proper scrutiny.

Despite relying on established Value-at-Risk (VaR) frameworks, the bank incurred losses exceeding $6 billion due to large, concentrated positions in credit derivatives that were not adequately captured by standard risk metrics.

docs.title: Core Problem
docs.text:
At the center of the failure was a combination of:

  • Overreliance on Value-at-Risk (VaR) as a primary risk metric
  • Underestimation of tail risk in portfolio return distributions
  • Significant concentration in illiquid credit positions
  • Inadequate internal controls and oversight of risk limits

Although reported risk measures appeared manageable, they failed to capture the magnitude of potential extreme losses.

docs.title: Analytical Approach
docs.text:
Using a simulated credit derivatives portfolio, the analysis evaluates:

  • Value-at-Risk (VaR) across parametric, historical, and Monte Carlo methods
  • Expected Shortfall (ES) as a complementary tail risk measure
  • Differences in risk estimates under pre-stress and stress conditions
  • Distributional characteristics of returns, including extreme tail behavior

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• VaR estimates remained relatively stable even under stress conditions
  • Expected Shortfall (ES) increased significantly, revealing large tail losses
  • The distribution of returns exhibited negative skew and fat tails
  • Stress scenarios exposed losses far exceeding VaR thresholds

These results demonstrate that standard VaR measures can severely understate risk in the presence of extreme events.

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text:
VaR measures the probability of loss up to a threshold, but does not capture the magnitude of losses beyond that point.

This limitation makes VaR particularly unreliable in environments characterized by tail risk and market stress.

docs.title: Implications for Risk Management
docs.text:
• Firms must supplement VaR with tail-sensitive measures such as Expected Shortfall
  • Concentration risk must be monitored alongside statistical risk metrics
  • Stress testing should play a central role in risk assessment
  • Risk governance must ensure that model outputs are critically evaluated—not accepted mechanically

This block performs Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the daily changes of the yield curve across 10 maturities to identify the primary drivers of yield curve movements:

  4. vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(S): Performs eigen decomposition on the covariance matrix S to obtain eigenvalues (vals) and eigenvectors (vecs). Eigenvalues represent the amount of variance explained by each principal component, and eigenvectors represent the directions (loadings) of these components.
  5. idx = np.argsort(vals)[::-1]: Sorts the eigenvalues in descending order to identify the principal components that explain the most variance.
  6. vals, vecs = vals[idx], vecs[:,idx]: Reorders both eigenvalues and eigenvectors according to the sorted eigenvalues.

docs.title: Context: Why LTCM Matters¶
docs.text:
Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) was one of the most sophisticated hedge funds of its time, founded by traders and Nobel laureates.

The fund pursued convergence trades—positions that expected small pricing differences between similar securities to disappear over time.

These trades were:

  • Highly leveraged
  • Assumed stable relationships across markets
  • Considered low-risk under normal conditions

However, in 1998, during a period of global financial stress, these assumptions broke down—leading to losses so severe that LTCM required a coordinated bailout.

docs.title: Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) — Model Risk Failure
Executive Summary
docs.text:
Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) represents one of the most prominent failures of quantitative risk modeling in modern financial history.

The fund relied on convergence trades supported by statistical models that assumed stable relationships across markets. While these models performed well under normal conditions, they failed catastrophically during periods of systemic stress.

docs.title: Core Problem
docs.text:
LTCM’s failure was driven by a combination of:

  • Extreme leverage applied to small-edge trades
  • Assumptions of stable correlations and volatility
  • Reliance on models calibrated to historical norms

When market conditions deviated sharply in 1998, these assumptions simultaneously broke down.

docs.title: Analytical Approach
docs.text:
Using yield curve data (1997–1998), the analysis evaluates:

  • Volatility regime changes using rolling and EWMA methods
  • Principal components of the yield curve (shift, twist, curvature)
  • Differences between base and stress environments
  • Value-at-Risk (VaR) estimates versus realized outcomes

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• Volatility increased rapidly during the crisis, exceeding model expectations
  • Correlations across positions moved toward one, eliminating diversification benefits
  • VaR estimates significantly understated potential losses
  • Leverage amplified relatively small model errors into systemic exposure

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text: LTCM did not fail because models were incorrect in form, but because they were applied under assumptions that did not hold in stress conditions.

docs.title: Implications for Risk Management
docs.text:
• Risk models must incorporate regime shifts, not just historical data
  • Correlation assumptions should be stress-tested explicitly
  • Leverage should be evaluated relative to model uncertainty
  • Scenario analysis is essential alongside statistical measures

docs.title: ✅ Scenario 3 — Reverse Stress Test (Viability Threshold)¶
docs.text:
Unlike the forward-looking scenarios, this reverse stress test identifies the conditions under which the bank's CET1 ratio would fall below a critical threshold of 4.5%. It uncovers the 'breaking points' for the bank:

  • Failure Thresholds: It determines that a corporate default rate increase of +6. 8 pp, a CRE decline of more than 42%, funding cost increases of +110 bps, or a market liquidity reduction of 40% are sufficient to breach the CET1 threshold.
  • Losses: The total losses required to push CET1 below 4.5% are 8.1B, and the reverse scenario itself produces 8.4B in losses. Critically, this results in a post-stress CET1 ratio of 4.3%, which breaches the 4.5% viability threshold.

  • Corporate defaults: +6.8 pp
  • CRE decline: >42%
  • Funding costs: +110 bps
  • Market liquidity: –40%

Computed Losses

  • Required to breach CET1: 8.1B
  • Reverse scenario produces: 8.4B
  • Post-stress CET1: 4.3% (breach)

docs.title: Sunrise National Bank (SNB) — Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis
Executive Summary
docs.text:
The SNB case illustrates how forward-looking stress testing reveals vulnerabilities that remain hidden under normal conditions.

While the bank appears adequately capitalized in baseline scenarios, stress testing exposes significant deterioration driven by credit losses, market shocks, and liquidity stress.

docs.title: Core Problem
docs.text:
• Reliance on baseline capital ratios
  • Underestimation of stress interactions
  • Insufficient integration of liquidity and market risks
  • Limited visibility into extreme scenarios

docs.title: Analytical Approach
docs.text:
The case evaluates:

  • Multiple stress scenarios (CRE collapse, supervisory adverse, reverse stress)
  • Loss composition across portfolios
  • CET1 capital deterioration
  • Reverse stress testing to identify viability thresholds

docs.title: Key Findings
docs.text:
• CET1 declines sharply under stress (~4.8%, ~3.1%, ~4.3%)
  • Supervisory scenario breaches regulatory capital requirements
  • Credit losses dominate total losses
  • Liquidity stress and counterparty exposure amplify impacts

docs.title: Key Insight
docs.text: Stress testing reveals risks that are invisible in baseline or historical models.

docs.title: Position Within Risk Framework
docs.text:
• LTCM → Model failure
  • Lehman → Liquidity failure
  • London Whale → Measurement failure
  • GFC → Systemic interaction
  • Knight → Operational and model risk failure
  • SNB → Forward-looking risk design

docs.title: Implication for Risk Management
docs.text:
• Firms must adopt forward-looking stress testing frameworks
  • Capital adequacy must be evaluated under extreme conditions
  • Liquidity risk must be integrated with credit and market risk
  • Reverse stress testing should identify failure thresholds proactively
